h: From tax collectors to Van Gogh's bandaged ear
p: For a building that's now all about creativity, Somerset House has a surprisingly official past. The grand quadrangle was built to house government offices, including the Navy Board and departments dealing with taxes and records, so generations of clerks once worked where artists and designers now gather. Look out for the grand staircase and the old vaults as you explore, which hint at the building's working life.

The Courtauld Gallery deserves a proper slice of your visit. It's not huge, which is exactly why it's so enjoyable, and it's crammed with famous paintings. Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère, with its puzzling mirror, is a real highlight, and Van Gogh's Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear hangs here too, along with works by Cézanne, Gauguin, Renoir and many more. Give it an hour or so on its own and you'll come away buzzing.

Out on the river terrace, the views east along the Thames towards the City and St Paul's are lovely, and it's a nice place for a drink when the weather plays ball. The building's various cafés and restaurants mean you can easily stretch a visit into a long lunch.

The Strand outside has a few treats of its own. Twinings has been selling tea from the same spot on the Strand since the early 1700s, and the Royal Courts of Justice, all Gothic towers and spires, are just a short walk east. Head the other way and Covent Garden's piazza, street performers and market are a few minutes' stroll, so you can easily turn this into a full day out in the West End.
